Maximum Protection.summary: Lock the doors first. At this age the goal is no contact with strangers, no spending, and content well inside their age rating.
principles: Chat with people they don’t know: off
Content: the most restrictive setting available
Play together where you can, so the rules feel shared rather than imposed

High Protection.summary: Still tightly controlled, but start explaining the reasons. Kids this age notice restrictions and will work around ones they don’t understand.
principles: Chat limited to friends you’ve both agreed on
Content one notch above the youngest setting
Agree screen time together rather than announcing it

Balanced Supervision.summary: Teens need some room. Keep the safety rails that matter most (strangers, spending, sleep) and loosen the rest.
principles: Spending limits rather than a hard block
Visibility over surveillance: you see patterns, not private messages

Guided Independence.summary: They’re close to managing this themselves. Focus on the few settings that prevent real harm and on the habits they’ll keep after 18.
principles: Keep location and sleep protections on
Talk through privacy settings rather than setting them silently
Make sure they know how to block, report, and come to you

helpModes.label: Quick setup
helpModes.hint: Just tell me what to tap.

helpModes.label: Review my settings
helpModes.hint: I’ve set things up. Check my work.

helpModes.label: I can’t find it
helpModes.hint: The menu doesn’t look like the instructions.

roblox.name: Roblox
roblox.blurb: A platform of millions of user-made games. The games themselves are made by other users, so quality and content vary enormously.
risks: Open chat means adults can talk to your child inside games
Robux spending adds up fast, often through gift cards
Content ratings are set by creators, so some games slip through
beforeYouStart: You’ll need your own Roblox account, linked to your child’s, to change these settings.
Have your child’s login handy, and pick a Parent PIN they don’t know.

steps.title: Check which account they are on
steps.why: Since June 2026 the account type decides what your child can see and who can reach them, before any setting you change.
do: Look at the account type shown for your child.
Roblox Kids is for 5 to 8. It shows only pre-screened Minimal and Mild experiences, and chat is off until you switch it on from your linked account.
Roblox Select is for 9 to 15 and goes up to Moderate.
If the type looks wrong for their age, verify yourself as a parent so Roblox can place them properly.

recommended.7-11: Roblox Kids to age 8, then Roblox Select

steps.note: Control loosens in stages, not all at once. At 13 they take over their own privacy and chat settings, and at 18 the account unlinks from you automatically. Roblox says the exact ages and features vary by region.

steps.title: Link your account and set a Parent PIN
steps.why: Without a PIN, your child can undo everything you’re about to set in about ten seconds.
do: Sign in to your child’s Roblox account on a phone or at roblox.com.
Open Settings, then Parental Controls.
Add your own email as the parent email and verify it from your inbox.
Create a Parent PIN. Choose something your child won’t guess, and not a birthday.
steps.result: Every setting below now requires your PIN to change.

steps.title: Set Content Maturity
steps.why: This is the single biggest lever. It filters which games your child can even open.
steps.path: Settings → Parental Controls → [your child] → Settings You Manage → Content restrictions → Content maturity
do: Open Content restrictions, then Content maturity.
Pick the level for your child’s age from the table.
Confirm with your PIN.
steps.note: The four levels are Minimal, Mild, Moderate and Restricted. Restricted is for age-verified adults only and includes strong violence and realistic blood.

steps.title: Control who can talk to them
steps.why: Most of the real risk on Roblox is contact, not content. This is the step worth getting right.
steps.path: Settings → Parental Controls → Settings You Manage → Communication
do: Open the Communication section.
Set each of Game chat, Direct chat, Friends chat and Party to the level below.
Confirm with your PIN.
steps.note: Direct chat needs a parent’s consent for under-13s, and game chat is restricted for under-9s by default. Party features are limited to age-checked 13+ users.

steps.title: Put a ceiling on Robux spending
steps.why: In-game purchases are designed to be quick and frictionless. A monthly cap turns an expensive surprise into a small one.
steps.path: Settings → Parental Controls → Settings You Manage → Spending restrictions
do: Open Spending restrictions.
Set a monthly spend limit you’re comfortable with.
Turn on transaction notifications so you see purchases as they happen.

recommended.13-15: A small monthly cap you agree together

steps.note: Roblox also sends high-spend alerts at $100, $250 and $500.

steps.title: Set a daily time limit
steps.why: Roblox has no natural stopping point. A built-in limit avoids the nightly argument.
steps.path: Settings → Parental Controls → Screen time → Manage → Screen time limit
do: Open Screen time, then Manage.
Choose a daily limit.
While you’re here, look at the list of the top games they played this week. It’s a good conversation starter.

steps.title: Go through the friends list together
steps.why: Friend lists collect strangers over time. Ten minutes here is worth more than any setting.
do: Open your child’s friends list.
Ask about anyone you don’t recognize: where did you meet them?
Remove anyone they only know from inside a game.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: Roblox settings only cover Roblox. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time (iPhone/iPad/Mac), Family Link (Android/Chromebook), Microsoft Family Safety (Windows/Xbox), or your console’s parental controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Parent PIN set and known only to you
Content maturity set for their age
Chat restricted to friends, or off
talkAboutIt: Ask them to show you their favorite game and play a round with them.
Agree what they’ll do if someone asks them to move the chat to Discord or Snapchat. That’s a common grooming step.
Make sure they know nobody legitimate ever needs their password or a free-Robux code.

kidsAlt.name: Roblox Kids and Roblox Select
kidsAlt.what: New in June 2026. Roblox Kids is for 5 to 8 and shows only pre-screened Minimal and Mild experiences, with chat off unless you switch it on from a linked parent account. Roblox Select covers 9 to 15 and goes up to Moderate.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Which one they get is decided by Roblox's age check or by you verifying yourself as a parent. Control loosens in stages: at 13 they take over their own privacy and chat settings, and at 18 the account unlinks from you automatically.
kidsAlt.countryNote: Worldwide, though Roblox says the exact ages and features vary by region.

tiktok.name: TikTok
tiktok.blurb: Short video feed driven by an algorithm. The feed adapts fast, which is both the appeal and the risk.
risks: The algorithm can narrow quickly onto body image, diet or self-harm content
Public accounts invite comments and messages from strangers
It is genuinely hard to stop watching, which eats into sleep
beforeYouStart: TikTok’s minimum age is 13. If your child is younger, the honest answer is that they’re on the wrong app rather than the wrong settings.
You’ll need TikTok installed on your own phone, and your child’s phone in your hand for about a minute.

steps.title: Set up Family Pairing
steps.why: Family Pairing lets you change your teen’s safety settings from your own phone, and stops them changing them back.
steps.path: Profile → ☰ (top right) → Settings and privacy → Family Pairing
do: On your phone: open your profile, tap the three lines top right, then Settings and privacy.
Scroll to Family Pairing and tap Continue.
Choose Parent. You’ll get a QR code.
On your teen’s phone: go to the same Family Pairing screen, choose Teen, and scan your QR code.
Your teen reviews the permissions and taps Link accounts.
steps.result: Everything below is now set from your phone.

steps.title: Make the account private
steps.why: A public account means anyone can see their videos, comment, and work out where they go to school.
steps.path: Family Pairing → [your teen] → Privacy and safety
do: Turn Private account on.
Turn off Suggest your teen’s account to others.

steps.title: Limit messages, comments and mentions
steps.why: This is where strangers actually reach teenagers. Content filters don’t help with contact.
steps.path: Family Pairing → [your teen] → Privacy and safety → Safety
do: Set who can send direct messages.
Set who can comment on their videos.
Set who can mention or tag them.

recommended.13-15: Friends, or No one for DMs

steps.note: Direct messaging is switched off entirely for accounts registered as under 16.

steps.title: Turn on Restricted Mode and keyword filters
steps.why: Restricted Mode filters out content that isn’t appropriate for younger viewers. Keyword filters let you name the specific things you’re worried about.
do: Turn Restricted Mode on.
Open Filter video keywords and add words relevant to your family. Diet and body-image terms are a common starting point.

steps.title: Set daily screen time and a Time away schedule
steps.why: TikTok’s feed has no end. The sleep effect is the most reliably harmful part for most teenagers.
do: Set a Daily screen time limit (the minimum TikTok allows is 40 minutes).
Add a Time away schedule covering school hours and bedtime.

recommended.13-15: 60 minutes, phone out of the bedroom overnight
recommended.16-17: Agree a limit together, keep the overnight block

steps.title: Show them how to reset the feed
steps.why: If the algorithm goes somewhere dark, they can fix it themselves. Teaching this beats monitoring it.
do: Show them the 'not interested' option on a long-press of any video.
Show them Settings and privacy → Content preferences → Refresh your For You feed.
Agree that if the feed gets strange, they tell you and you fix it together, with no blame.

checklist: DMs and comments limited to friends
Daily limit and overnight Time away set
They know how to reset the feed and report a video
talkAboutIt: Ask what’s on their For You page right now. It’s the fastest way to know what they’re seeing.
Agree that filters and screenshots of DMs come to you without anyone getting in trouble.
Talk about why an account being private matters even when the videos seem harmless.

kidsAlt.name: The Under 13 Experience
kidsAlt.what: In the United States only, TikTok runs a separate under-13 version that collects less and adds extra protections. Everywhere else, including the UK, Ireland and Canada, TikTok's terms say the service is for 13 and over and there is no younger option.
kidsAlt.watchOut: We could not read TikTok's children's privacy page to confirm what it does and does not let a child do, so treat the detail as unconfirmed and check it yourself.

instagram.name: Instagram
instagram.blurb: Photo, video and messaging app. Under-18 accounts now get a protected 'Teen Account' setup by default.
risks: Contact from adults through DMs and story replies
Comparison and body-image pressure, especially in Reels
Location and school details leaking through tags and photos
beforeYouStart: Check the birthday on their account first. Teen Account protections only apply if Instagram knows they’re under 18. A wrong birthday quietly disables all of it.
You’ll both need an Instagram account for supervision.

steps.title: Check the birthday on the account is correct
steps.why: This is the step most people skip, and it undoes everything else. Teen Accounts are applied based on the stated age.
steps.path: Profile → ☰ → Settings and privacy → Accounts Center → Personal details
do: Open their profile and check the date of birth on the account.
If it’s wrong, correct it. Instagram may ask for verification.
steps.result: With a correct under-18 birthday, sensitive content filters, restricted DMs, a 60-minute daily reminder and overnight Sleep Mode all switch on automatically.

steps.title: Set up parental supervision
steps.why: Teen Accounts protect. Supervision gives you visibility, and for under-16s, approval rights over setting changes.
steps.path: Settings and privacy → Supervision (or Family Center)
do: On your account, open Settings and privacy, then Supervision.
Tap Set up supervision and send the invitation to your teen.
Your teen opens the invitation and accepts it.
Either of you can start the invite, and sometimes it’s easier if they invite you.
steps.note: You’ll see who they follow, who follows them, accounts they’ve interacted with recently, and daily screen time. You won’t see the content of their messages.

steps.title: Know what needs your approval (under 16)
steps.why: For under-16s, loosening a safety setting sends you a request. Expect a few, and treat each one as a conversation rather than a yes/no.
do: Watch for approval requests in Supervision.
When one comes in, ask why they want the change before deciding.

steps.title: Tighten messaging and comments
steps.why: DMs are the main route strangers use. Teen Accounts already restrict this, but it’s worth confirming.
steps.path: Settings and privacy → Messages and story replies / Comments
do: Confirm messages are limited to people they follow.
Turn on Hidden Words to filter offensive comments and message requests.
Set story replies to People you follow.

steps.title: Confirm the account is private and location is off
steps.why: A private account plus no location tags is most of the privacy job done.
do: Confirm Private account is on.
Turn off location tags when posting.
Check their bio doesn’t name their school or team.

steps.title: Check screen time and Sleep Mode
steps.why: Sleep Mode mutes notifications and auto-replies to DMs overnight. It’s the setting most likely to actually improve things.
do: Confirm Sleep Mode is on (default is 10pm to 8am).
Set a daily time limit if you want a firmer stop.

steps.title: Scroll the follower list together
steps.why: Follower lists are where the surprises live. Do this one together rather than behind their back.
do: Open their followers list and scroll it with them.
Remove or block anyone they can’t place.
Show them how to block and report while you’re there.

checklist: Birthday on the account is correct
DMs limited to people they follow
talkAboutIt: Ask who they message most. You’ll learn more from that than from any dashboard.
Agree what happens if an adult they don’t know messages them: screenshot, don’t reply, show you.
Talk about how edited and filtered the feed is, without lecturing.
instagram.noKidsAlt: Instagram Kids was announced in 2021, paused, and never launched. Teen Accounts start at 13, so there is nothing here for a younger child.

snapchat.name: Snapchat
snapchat.blurb: Messaging app built around disappearing photos and videos, plus a live location map.
risks: Snap Map can broadcast their exact location to a wide friends list
Messages disappear, so evidence of harassment disappears too
Quick Add surfaces strangers as suggested friends
beforeYouStart: You need your own Snapchat account, and you need to be friends with your child on it before Family Center will work.
Family Center shows you who they talk to, not what they say. That’s deliberate, and worth explaining to your child.

steps.title: Add each other as friends
steps.why: Family Center only works between accounts that are already friends.
do: On your account, tap Add Friends and search your child’s username.
Have them accept.

steps.title: Set up Family Center
steps.why: It shows you their contacts from the last week and lets you report accounts directly to Snapchat.
steps.path: Profile → ⚙️ Settings → Privacy Control → Family Center
do: Open your profile, tap the gear icon, then Privacy Control, then Family Center.
Select your child’s name and send the invitation.
On their phone, they tap View Invitation, then Accept.
steps.result: You’ll see who they’ve messaged in the last seven days and their friends list.

steps.title: Turn on Ghost Mode
steps.why: Snap Map shows live location to everyone on their friends list. For most children this is the single most important setting on Snapchat.
do: From the camera screen, tap the location pin at the bottom left to open the Map.
Tap the gear icon in the top right.
Turn on Ghost Mode.

recommended.13-15: Ghost Mode on, or share with a small chosen list
recommended.16-17: Agree together — at minimum, not 'My Friends'

steps.title: Limit who can contact them and see their story
steps.why: Default settings are more open than most parents expect.
do: Open Contact Me and set it to Friends.
Open View My Story and set it to My Friends, or a Custom list.
Turn off Quick Add so they stop being suggested to strangers.

steps.title: Restrict sensitive content in Stories and Spotlight
steps.why: Discover and Spotlight are public feeds, and they’re where most of the age-inappropriate content sits.
do: In Family Center, open Content Controls.
Turn on the restriction for sensitive content.

steps.title: Talk about the disappearing part
steps.why: Children often believe a snap is gone forever. It isn’t. Anyone can screenshot or photograph the screen with another phone.
do: Explain that anything sent can be saved by the person receiving it.
Agree that if they’re ever sent something upsetting, they screenshot it before it disappears and show you.

checklist: They know how to screenshot and report
talkAboutIt: Ask them to show you their Snap Map and who can see them.
Agree the rule that disappearing doesn’t mean private.
Make sure they know they can block someone without explaining themselves to anyone.
snapchat.noKidsAlt: Snapchat's minimum is 13 and there is no younger version. Family Center is for 13 to 17 and the teenager has to accept the invite.

discord.name: Discord
discord.blurb: Text and voice chat organized into servers. Popular alongside gaming, and largely made up of communities of strangers.
risks: Public servers put your child in rooms with adults they don’t know
Voice chat leaves no record
It’s a common place for someone met in a game to move the conversation
beforeYouStart: Discord now applies teen-appropriate settings by default to accounts registered as under 18, but you should still check them.
Family Center linking is done from your teen’s side. They generate a QR code that you scan with the Discord mobile app.

steps.title: Turn on Family Center and link your accounts
steps.why: It gives you a weekly picture of who they’re talking to and which servers they’ve joined.
do: Both of you: open User Settings and find the Family Center tab (on mobile, tap your profile icon first).
Turn on Enable Family Center tab.
Your teen opens Family Center and chooses Connect with Guardian to generate a QR code.
Scan that code with the Discord mobile app on your phone.
Your teen accepts the connection.
steps.result: You’ll see new friends added, users messaged, servers joined and call durations for the last 7 days, plus a weekly email. You won’t see message content.

steps.title: Set the sensitive content filter
steps.why: Direct messages and server messages can contain images your child didn’t ask for.
do: Open Privacy & Safety.
Set sensitive content in direct messages to Block.
Set sensitive content in servers to Block.

steps.title: Close down direct messages from strangers
steps.why: By default, sharing a server with someone can be enough for them to message your child privately.
do: Turn off Allow direct messages from server members.
Set who can send friend requests to Friends of Friends, or off entirely.
Turn off Message Requests if you’d rather nothing gets through at all.

recommended.13-15: Server DMs off, friend requests from friends of friends only

steps.title: Go through their server list together
steps.why: This is the part that matters most and no setting can do it for you. Most risk on Discord comes from which rooms they’re in.
do: Open their server list and ask about each one: what is it, who’s in it, how did you find it?
Leave any large public server they can’t explain.
Agree that new servers get mentioned to you.

steps.title: Set a monthly spending cap
steps.why: Nitro subscriptions and gifts are easy to rack up.
do: Set a monthly limit on purchases.

steps.title: Set screen time limits
steps.why: Voice chat sessions run long, especially at night.
do: Schedule downtime, particularly overnight.

talkAboutIt: Ask which server they spend the most time in and what they like about it.
Agree that if anyone asks them to move to a private DM or another app, they tell you.
Make sure they know how to block and report inside Discord.
discord.noKidsAlt: Discord's minimum is 13 and there is no younger version. Family Center is built for teenagers, the teen has to agree to it, and they can disconnect it.

youtube.name: YouTube
youtube.blurb: The biggest video platform. Which version your child should use depends heavily on their age.
risks: Autoplay and recommendations pull children well past what they set out to watch
Comments sections are unmoderated in practice
Content aimed at adults is often styled to look child-friendly
beforeYouStart: There are three options: YouTube Kids (young children), a supervised YouTube account through Family Link (roughly 9+), and a normal account (13+).
You’ll need the Family Link app, or access to families.google.com.

steps.title: Choose the right version of YouTube
steps.why: Getting this right matters more than any individual toggle.
do: Under about 9: use the YouTube Kids app instead.
Roughly 9 to 12: use a supervised YouTube account via Family Link.
13 and over: a normal account, with the settings below applied.

recommended.0-6: YouTube Kids, or a supervised account on Explore
recommended.7-11: YouTube Kids, or a supervised account on Explore
recommended.13-15: Supervised account or normal account with limits
recommended.16-17: Normal account, with a conversation about the feed

steps.title: Set the content level
steps.why: This decides which slice of YouTube they can reach. It’s the main control on a supervised account.
steps.path: Family Link app → [your child] → Controls → Content restrictions → YouTube
do: Open Family Link and select your child.
Go to Controls, Content restrictions, then YouTube.
Pick the content setting for their age.
steps.note: The three levels are Explore (9+), Explore more (13+) and Most of YouTube (older teens). Supervised accounts can read comments but not post them.

steps.title: Turn off autoplay and pause history
steps.why: Autoplay is what turns a ten-minute video into two hours. Pausing history slows down the recommendation loop.
do: Turn Autoplay off.
Pause watch history and search history.
Clear the existing history if the recommendations have already drifted.

steps.title: Block channels you don’t want
steps.why: Faster than trying to filter by topic, and it sticks.
do: On a video from a channel you want gone, open the menu and choose Block this channel.
You can also manage blocked channels from the parent settings.

steps.title: Set a time limit at the device level
steps.why: YouTube doesn’t have its own strong time limit, so use Screen Time or Family Link.
do: iPhone/iPad: Settings → Screen Time → App Limits.
Android/Chromebook: Family Link → Controls → Daily limit.

checklist: Right version of YouTube for their age
Time limit set at device level
talkAboutIt: Watch a couple of their favorite creators with them and ask what they like.
Talk about sponsorship and why creators recommend things.
Agree what they do if a video makes them uncomfortable: close it and tell you, rather than keep watching.

links.label: YouTube — content settings for supervised accounts (official)
Google — YouTube & YouTube Kids options for your child (official)
YouTube — parental controls for supervised accounts (official)

kidsAlt.name: YouTube Kids
kidsAlt.what: A separate app with its own content levels for preschool, younger and older children, or a list you approve yourself. A child under 13 on a supervised Google account can only use this one, not the main YouTube.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Search is switched on by default. Turn it off and they are limited to channels YouTube Kids has verified. Supervision also ends automatically on their 13th birthday.
kidsAlt.countryNote: Available in all four countries here, though not in Quebec.

fortnite.name: Fortnite
fortnite.blurb: Online shooter with cartoon violence, played in squads with voice chat. Controls sit in two places: Epic’s account and the console or device.
risks: Open voice chat with random squadmates, including adults
V-Bucks spending, often through gift cards
Battle pass mechanics that reward daily play and make missing a day feel costly
beforeYouStart: Choose a 6-digit PIN before you start. It’s shared with the Epic Games Store.
You’ll need to set controls in Fortnite and again on the console or device. Neither covers the other.

steps.title: Set the parental controls PIN
steps.why: Everything else depends on this. Without it, the settings are suggestions.
do: From the main menu, open the three-line menu, then the gear icon.
Choose Parental Controls.
Create a 6-digit PIN. Don’t reuse a PIN your child already knows.
Confirm the email address that receives reports.

steps.title: Set voice and text chat
steps.why: This is the biggest one. Random squad fill puts your child in a voice channel with strangers by default.
steps.path: Parental Controls → Voice Chat / Text Chat
do: Set Voice Chat and Text Chat to the level below.
Confirm with your PIN.

recommended.16-17: Friends Only, or Friends & Teammates if agreed

steps.note: The options are Nobody, Friends Only, Friends & Teammates, and Everybody.

steps.title: Turn on the mature language filter
steps.why: Replaces swearing in text chat with heart symbols. Small thing, easy win.
do: Toggle Filter Mature Language on.

steps.title: Require your PIN to add friends
steps.why: It turns every new friend request into a two-second conversation, which is exactly what you want.
steps.path: Parental Controls → Require a PIN to add Epic friends
do: Turn it on.

steps.title: Set playtime limits and weekly reports
steps.why: Fortnite matches don’t end at a convenient moment. A scheduled limit avoids the 'one more game' loop.
do: Set a daily limit (adjustable in 15-minute increments).
Set a different schedule for weekends if that suits you.
Turn on Weekly Playtime Reports so you get an email summary.

steps.title: Require your PIN for purchases
steps.why: V-Bucks purchases are two taps away otherwise.
steps.path: Epic Games Store settings → Parental Controls → require PIN for purchases
do: In the Epic Games Store parental controls, turn on the requirement for a PIN on all purchases.
Remove any saved payment card if your child plays unsupervised.

steps.title: Set the console or device controls too
steps.why: Epic’s controls don’t govern the console’s own chat and spending. Both layers are needed.
do: PlayStation: set communication and spending limits in Family Management.
Xbox: set Privacy & online safety and spending in Microsoft Family Safety.
Switch: set restriction level and play-time limits in the Parental Controls app.
iPhone/iPad: use Screen Time. Android: use Family Link.
steps.note: SafeStart has a guide for each console. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Playtime limit and weekly report on
Console or device controls also set
talkAboutIt: Ask who they usually squad up with, and whether they’ve ever played with someone they only know online.
Agree the rule: nobody in a game ever needs to know your real name, school or where you live.
Watch a match with them. It tells you more than any setting screen.

kidsAlt.name: A Cabined Account
kidsAlt.form: an account type in Epic Games
kidsAlt.what: Epic switches this on when a player gives an age under 13, or under the local age of digital consent where that is higher. Voice and text chat with other players, real-money purchases, custom display names and account linking are all off.
kidsAlt.watchOut: It gates the account, not the game. The content they see is the same. It lifts on its own when they reach the local age, or sooner if you give consent by email.

minecraft.name: Minecraft
minecraft.blurb: Building and survival game. Single player is about as safe as gaming gets. Multiplayer servers and Realms are where the controls matter.
risks: Public servers have open chat and no reliable moderation
Third-party servers and mods sit outside Microsoft’s controls entirely
Marketplace purchases with Minecoins
beforeYouStart: Most Minecraft controls actually live in the Microsoft account, not in the game. Set up a child account inside your family group first.
Single-player and a private Realm with known friends is a genuinely low-risk setup. Public servers are a different thing.

steps.title: Put them on a child Microsoft account inside your family
steps.why: Nothing else works without this. An adult account can’t be supervised.
do: Go to family.microsoft.com and sign in with your own Microsoft account.
Add your child as a family member, with their correct date of birth.
Make sure Minecraft is signed in with that account.

steps.title: Set multiplayer and communication in Xbox privacy settings
steps.why: These three toggles control who can reach your child inside Minecraft, on every platform.
steps.path: account.xbox.com/settings → [your child] → Privacy & online safety → Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, and Windows 10 devices
do: Go to account.xbox.com/settings and sign in with your parent account.
Select your child’s profile, then the Privacy & online safety tab.
Choose the Xbox and Windows devices section.
Set 'You can join multiplayer games', 'Others can communicate with voice, text, or invites' and 'You can add friends' to the levels below.

recommended.0-6: Multiplayer: Allow (for Realms with known friends). Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block.
recommended.7-11: Multiplayer: Allow (for Realms with known friends). Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block.
recommended.11-12: Multiplayer: Allow. Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block.
recommended.13-15: Multiplayer: Allow. Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Allow.

steps.title: Turn chat off inside the game as well
steps.why: Two layers is better than one, and the in-game setting covers cases the account setting doesn’t.
do: In Minecraft, open Settings and look for the chat option in the profile or general settings.
Turn chat off, or set it to show only commands, for younger children.
steps.note: The exact menu name moves between Minecraft versions. If you can’t find it, the Xbox privacy setting above is the one that matters. Check the official Minecraft help link below.

steps.title: Prefer a private Realm over public servers
steps.why: A Realm is invite-only and controlled by whoever owns it. Public servers are open to anyone.
do: If they want to play with friends, set up or join a Realm rather than a public server.
As the Realm owner, you control the invite list.
Talk about third-party servers — those sit entirely outside these controls.

steps.title: Require approval for purchases
steps.why: The Minecraft Marketplace sells skins and worlds for Minecoins, and children are the target market.
do: Turn on 'Needs organizer approval to buy things'.
Turn on purchase notification emails.

steps.title: Set screen time in Microsoft Family Safety
steps.why: Covers Minecraft across Xbox and Windows in one place.
do: Set daily limits or a schedule, per device.

checklist: Child account inside your Microsoft family
Multiplayer and communication set to friends only
Chat restricted in game for younger children
Playing on Realms rather than public servers
talkAboutIt: Ask them to give you a tour of what they’ve built. It’s an easy in.
Agree that public servers get checked with you first.
Talk about mods and downloads — where they come from matters.

links.label: Xbox — privacy and online safety settings (official)

kidsAlt.name: A Microsoft child account
kidsAlt.form: an account type in your family group
kidsAlt.what: Minecraft treats any account under 16 in the US and EU as a child account. From the family group you control multiplayer, Realms, friends, and who can talk to them by voice or text.
kidsAlt.watchOut: The controls live in Microsoft Family Safety rather than in Minecraft, which is why they get missed. They also do not apply to versions before 1.16.4, or to modded installs.

iphone.name: iPhone
iphone.blurb: Apple’s controls live in Screen Time, and work best when the child is in your Family Sharing group.
risks: App Store downloads that bypass everything you’ve set up
The browser, which reaches everything the app controls don’t
Late-night use, which is the most consistently harmful pattern
beforeYouStart: Set up Family Sharing first and add your child’s Apple Account to your family group. Screen Time is far weaker without it.
Choose a Screen Time passcode that is not the phone’s unlock code and that your child doesn’t know.

steps.title: Add them to Family Sharing
steps.why: It lets you manage their phone from yours, and it’s what makes Ask to Buy possible.
do: On your iPhone, open Settings and tap your name.
Tap Family Sharing and add your child.
If they’re under 13, create a child Apple Account for them here.

steps.title: Set a Screen Time passcode
steps.why: Without a separate passcode, your child can turn all of this off in about fifteen seconds.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Change Screen Time Passcode
do: Open Settings, then Screen Time, then choose your child under Family.
Set a Screen Time passcode.
Use a different code from the phone unlock, and don’t use a birthday.

steps.title: Turn on Content & Privacy Restrictions
steps.why: This is the master switch that unlocks everything else.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Content & Privacy Restrictions
do: Open Content & Privacy Restrictions.
Enter your Screen Time passcode.
Toggle Content & Privacy Restrictions on.

steps.title: Require approval for downloads and purchases
steps.why: Otherwise every setting you choose is one free app download away from irrelevant.
steps.path: Content & Privacy Restrictions → iTunes & App Store Purchases
do: Set In-app Purchases to Don’t Allow.
Set Installing Apps and Deleting Apps according to the ages below.
Turn on Ask to Buy in Family Sharing so download requests come to your phone.

recommended.0-6: Installing apps: Don’t Allow. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.7-11: Installing apps: Don’t Allow. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.11-12: Installing apps: Ask to Buy. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.13-15: Installing apps: Ask to Buy. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.16-17: Installing apps: Allow. In-app purchases: Ask to Buy.

steps.title: Set content ratings and web filtering
steps.why: The browser is the widest open door on the phone. Web content filtering closes most of it.
steps.path: Content & Privacy Restrictions → App Store, Media, Web & Games
do: Set age ratings for apps, films, TV and music.
Open Web Content and choose the level below.
For younger children, Allowed Websites lets you list the only sites that work.

steps.title: Set Downtime and App Limits
steps.why: Downtime is the one that protects sleep, which is the change most families actually feel.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Downtime / App Limits
do: Set Downtime to cover overnight — school nights first if you want an easier start.
Add App Limits for the categories that run away with time, usually Social and Games.
Choose which apps stay available during Downtime under Always Allowed (phone and messages to you, at minimum).

recommended.0-6: Downtime from 7pm, Social and Games limited to 45 min
recommended.7-11: Downtime from 7pm, Social and Games limited to 45 min

steps.title: Lock down privacy and location changes
steps.why: Stops apps quietly gaining location or contacts access later.
do: Open Location Services and set it to Don’t Allow Changes after you’ve set it how you want.
Do the same for Contacts and Photos.
Turn on Communication Limits so contact during Downtime is restricted to known contacts.

checklist: Screen Time passcode set, and secret
Ask to Buy on, in-app purchases off
talkAboutIt: Tell them what you’ve set and why. Hidden controls get worked around; explained ones usually don’t.
Agree how they earn more freedom over time.
Show them how to report and block in the apps they use most.

links.label: Apple — Use parental controls on your child’s device (official)

ipad.name: iPad
ipad.blurb: Same Screen Time controls as iPhone. Worth setting separately, since iPads are more often shared and more often used for video.
risks: Shared iPads often sit on an adult account with no restrictions at all
Long-form video and games make time limits more important than on a phone
The browser reaches everything the app controls don’t
beforeYouStart: If the iPad is shared, decide whether it’s your child’s device (set it up under their Apple Account) or a family device (set restrictions on the account it uses).
Set up Family Sharing first and pick a Screen Time passcode your child doesn’t know.

steps.title: Add them to Family Sharing
steps.why: Lets you manage the iPad from your own phone and enables Ask to Buy.
do: On your device, open Settings and tap your name.
Tap Family Sharing and add your child.
Make sure the iPad is signed in to their Apple Account, not yours.

steps.title: Set a Screen Time passcode
steps.why: Otherwise every setting below can be switched off from the iPad itself.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Change Screen Time Passcode
do: Open Settings, then Screen Time.
Set a Screen Time passcode that differs from the unlock code.

steps.title: Turn on Content & Privacy Restrictions
steps.why: The master switch for content ratings, web filtering and purchases.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Content & Privacy Restrictions
do: Open Content & Privacy Restrictions and enter your passcode.
Toggle it on.

steps.title: Require approval for downloads and purchases
steps.why: iPads are where 'free' games with aggressive in-app purchases tend to land.
steps.path: Content & Privacy Restrictions → iTunes & App Store Purchases
do: Set In-app Purchases to Don’t Allow.
Set Installing Apps to match the ages below.
Turn on Ask to Buy so requests come to your phone.

recommended.0-6: Installing apps: Don’t Allow. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.7-11: Installing apps: Don’t Allow. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.11-12: Installing apps: Ask to Buy. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.13-15: Installing apps: Ask to Buy. In-app purchases: Don’t Allow.
recommended.16-17: Installing apps: Allow. In-app purchases: Ask to Buy.

steps.title: Set content ratings and web filtering
steps.why: Safari is the widest open door on the device.
steps.path: Content & Privacy Restrictions → App Store, Media, Web & Games
do: Set age ratings for apps, films, TV and music.
Open Web Content and pick the level below.
For younger children, Allowed Websites Only is much stronger than the adult filter.

steps.title: Set Downtime and App Limits
steps.why: iPads get used for hours without anyone noticing. Limits create a natural stop.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Downtime / App Limits
do: Set Downtime to cover the evening and overnight.
Add App Limits for video and games.
Use Always Allowed for anything that should still work, like messages to you.

recommended.0-6: Downtime from 7pm, 45 min on games and video
recommended.7-11: Downtime from 7pm, 45 min on games and video

checklist: iPad signed in to the child’s Apple Account
Screen Time passcode set and secret
Ask to Buy on, in-app purchases off
talkAboutIt: If the iPad is shared, agree who uses it when and for what.
Keep it out of the bedroom overnight if you can. It does more than any setting.
Tell them what you’ve set and why.

links.label: Apple — Use parental controls on your child’s device (official)

android.name: Android phone or tablet
android.blurb: Google’s Family Link supervises the child’s Google account and the device itself.
risks: Apps sideloaded outside the Play Store bypass Play’s age ratings
The browser reaches everything app controls don’t
Overnight use
beforeYouStart: You need to be 18+ with your own Google Account, and you and your child need to be in the same country.
Changes can take about five minutes to reach the device, so don’t panic if a setting doesn’t apply instantly.

steps.title: Set up Family Link supervision
steps.why: It’s the foundation. Nothing else in this guide works without it.
do: Install the Family Link app on your phone.
Create a Google Account for your child if they’re under 13, or add supervision to their existing account.
Follow the prompts on their device to link it. You’ll need the device in your hands.
steps.note: Family Link can supervise Android devices and Chromebooks. It cannot supervise iPhones or iPads.

steps.title: Control app downloads and approvals
steps.why: The quickest way for controls to become irrelevant is a new app you didn’t know about.
do: Turn on approval for all Play Store downloads, including free apps.
Set Play Store content ratings for apps, games, films and TV.
Review what’s already installed and block anything that shouldn’t be there.

recommended.0-6: Approval required for everything, apps rated PEGI 7 / ESRB E
recommended.7-11: Approval required for everything, apps rated PEGI 7 / ESRB E
recommended.11-12: Approval required for everything, apps rated PEGI 12 / ESRB E10+
recommended.13-15: Approval required for paid apps, ratings PEGI 12 / ESRB T

steps.title: Filter web and search
steps.why: Chrome is the widest opening on the device.
steps.path: Family Link → [your child] → Controls → Content restrictions → Google Chrome / Google Search
do: Set Chrome to Try to block explicit sites, or Only allow approved sites for younger children.
Turn SafeSearch on and lock it.
Add specific sites to allow or block as needed.

steps.title: Set daily limits and bedtime
steps.why: Bedtime is the setting that changes the most in practice.
steps.path: Family Link → [your child] → Controls → Daily limit / Bedtime
do: Set daily limits, which can differ by day of the week.
Set a bedtime schedule that locks the device.
You can grant bonus time from your phone when it’s genuinely warranted.

steps.title: Decide on location sharing
steps.why: Useful for younger children. For teenagers, worth agreeing rather than imposing.
do: Turn on location if you want it, and tell your child it’s on.
For older teens, discuss it first — covert tracking damages trust more than it protects.

steps.title: Set YouTube separately
steps.why: YouTube has its own content levels that sit inside Family Link.
steps.path: Family Link → [your child] → Controls → Content restrictions → YouTube
do: Choose the content setting: Explore (9+), Explore more (13+) or Most of YouTube.
Consider the YouTube Kids app instead for under-9s.

talkAboutIt: Show them the Family Link app so it isn’t a mystery.
Agree what happens when they want a new app, so it becomes a request rather than a fight.
Talk about sideloading if they’re technical enough to know the term.

links.label: Google — YouTube options for your child (official)

kidsAlt.name: Google Kids Space
kidsAlt.what: A child home screen with Play, Read, Watch and Make tabs, drawing on teacher-approved apps, chosen books and YouTube Kids. It sits on top of a supervised Google account made through Family Link.
kidsAlt.watchOut: It only comes pre-installed on certain tablets, among them Pixel Tablet, Lenovo, onn., Nokia, Medion and Multilaser. You cannot add it to any Android tablet, which is what catches most parents out.

windows.name: Windows PC
windows.blurb: Microsoft Family Safety covers Windows, Xbox and Edge from one dashboard.
risks: Web filtering only works in Microsoft Edge, so other browsers need blocking
A local (non-Microsoft) account bypasses everything
Game downloads and in-game spending
beforeYouStart: Your child needs their own child Microsoft account, signed in on the PC. If they use your account, none of this applies.
Web filtering is Edge-only. Plan to block other browsers, or the filter does nothing.

steps.title: Create a child account in your family group
steps.why: The foundation for everything else.
do: Go to family.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft account.
Add a family member, choosing the child option, with their correct date of birth.
On the PC, sign them in with that account and make sure they’re not using yours.

steps.title: Set content filters
steps.why: Blocks adult sites in Edge and sets age ratings for apps and games.
do: Turn on Filter inappropriate websites and searches.
Turn on Only use allowed browsers, which blocks Chrome, Firefox and others.
Under Apps and games, set the age rating limit.

steps.title: Set screen time
steps.why: You can set different limits per device, which helps if homework happens on the same PC.
do: Set a schedule for the Windows device.
Add separate app limits if a specific game is the problem rather than the PC itself.

steps.title: Require approval for purchases
steps.why: Stops surprise Microsoft Store and game purchases.
do: Turn on 'Needs organizer approval to buy things'.
Turn on email notifications for purchases.
Remove any saved card, or use a balance instead.

steps.title: Turn on activity reporting
steps.why: A weekly summary is a better conversation starter than a live feed.
do: Turn on activity reporting and weekly email summaries.
Tell your child it’s on. Reports work better as a shared thing.

checklist: Child Microsoft account created and in use
Web filtering on, other browsers blocked
App and game age ratings set
talkAboutIt: Agree homework time versus game time rather than one blanket limit.
Explain that the web filter only works in Edge, so switching browsers isn’t a loophole, it’s just blocked.
Look at the weekly report together.

mac.name: Mac
mac.blurb: Screen Time on macOS works much like iPhone, and syncs across devices signed in to the same Apple Account.
risks: Shared family Macs often run on an adult account with no controls
The browser reaches everything app controls don’t
Downloads outside the App Store
beforeYouStart: Give your child their own user account on the Mac, signed in to their own Apple Account inside your Family Sharing group.
macOS menu names shift between versions. If a menu doesn’t match, check Apple’s official page linked below.

steps.title: Give them their own login and add them to Family Sharing
steps.why: Screen Time applies per account. On a shared login it does nothing useful.
do: Create a separate user account on the Mac for your child.
Add their Apple Account to your Family Sharing group.
Sign them in to that account on the Mac.

steps.title: Turn on Screen Time and set a passcode
steps.why: The passcode is what stops them switching it off.
do: Open System Settings, then Screen Time.
Select your child under Family.
Turn on Lock Screen Time Settings and set a passcode they don’t know.

steps.title: Set content and privacy restrictions
steps.why: Covers web content, app ratings and store purchases.
do: Turn on Content & Privacy.
Under Content Restrictions, set web content to Limit Adult Websites, or Allowed Websites Only for younger children.
Set app and media age ratings.
Under Store Restrictions, turn off in-app purchases and require a password for every purchase.

steps.title: Set Downtime and App Limits
steps.why: Homework on a laptop makes a blanket limit unrealistic, so limit the categories that actually run away.
do: Set Downtime for the evening and overnight.
Add App Limits for Games and Social rather than everything.
Add anything they need for schoolwork to Always Allowed.

checklist: Child has their own Mac login
Screen Time locked with a passcode
talkAboutIt: Separate schoolwork from everything else so limits feel fair.
Agree where the laptop lives overnight.
Tell them what’s set rather than letting them discover it.

links.label: Apple — Use parental controls on your child’s device (official)

chromebook.name: Chromebook
chromebook.blurb: Managed through Family Link, the same as Android. School-issued Chromebooks are managed by the school instead.
risks: School-issued devices may already be managed, and your controls won’t apply
Everything runs in the browser, so web filtering matters more than app controls
Extensions can change how sites behave
beforeYouStart: If this is a school Chromebook, the school’s policies take priority and you may not be able to add supervision. Ask the school first.
Chromebook supervision needs Chrome OS 71 or later.

steps.title: Add your child’s account as supervised
steps.why: Supervision is what connects the Chromebook to Family Link.
do: Set up your child’s Google Account with supervision in Family Link.
On the Chromebook, sign in with that supervised account.
Make sure they aren’t signing in as a guest, which bypasses supervision.

steps.title: Filter the web and lock SafeSearch
steps.why: On a Chromebook, the browser is the device. This is the main control.
steps.path: Family Link → [your child] → Controls → Content restrictions → Google Chrome
do: Choose Try to block explicit sites, or Only allow approved sites for younger children.
Turn SafeSearch on and lock it.
Add specific allow or block entries as needed.

steps.title: Control apps and extensions
steps.why: Extensions are the Chromebook equivalent of installing software.
do: Require approval for Play Store downloads.
Review installed extensions and remove anything unfamiliar.
Decide whether they can install extensions at all.

steps.title: Set daily limits and bedtime
steps.why: Especially worth it if the Chromebook is also the homework machine.
steps.path: Family Link → [your child] → Controls → Daily limit / Bedtime
do: Set daily limits that vary by day if homework needs differ.
Set a bedtime that locks the device.

checklist: Supervised account signed in, guest mode not in use
talkAboutIt: If it’s a school device, check what the school already blocks so you’re not duplicating.
Agree homework time versus free time.
Explain that guest mode isn’t a workaround, because you’ll notice.

playstation.name: PlayStation
playstation.blurb: Controls are set by the Family Manager, either on the console or at playstation.com.
risks: Voice chat with strangers in online matches
PlayStation Store spending, including through wallet top-ups
Games rated well above the child’s age arriving through friends' recommendations
beforeYouStart: You need a PlayStation Network account in your own name to act as Family Manager.
Create a child account for your child rather than letting them use an adult one. This is the step that makes everything else possible.

steps.title: Set up Family Management and a child account
steps.why: Restrictions only apply to child accounts within your family.
do: Sign in at playstation.com/acct/family with your own account.
Add a family member and create a child account with their real date of birth.
Sign that account in on the console.

steps.title: Set age-level restrictions for games and content
steps.why: Blocks games above their rating from launching, which is more reliable than hoping you notice.
steps.path: Family Management → [your child] → Parental Controls → Age level for games
do: Set the age level for games to match their age.
Set the level for Blu-ray and DVD content.
Restrict or block the internet browser for younger children.

steps.title: Restrict communication and user-generated content
steps.why: This is the setting that governs voice chat, messages and shared content from strangers.
steps.path: Family Management → [your child] → Parental Controls → Communication and user-generated content
do: Restrict messaging and chat with other players.
Restrict the ability to view or share videos and images made by other players.

steps.title: Set play time limits
steps.why: PlayStation lets you set both a daily amount and a window of hours, which is useful for school nights.
steps.path: Family Management → [your child] → Play Time Settings
do: Set the hours of the day they can play.
Set a daily duration.
Choose whether the console logs them out at the limit or just warns them.
Note these settings apply to both PS5 and PS4.

steps.title: Set a monthly spending limit
steps.why: Wallet top-ups and in-game currency are where console spending usually escapes.
steps.path: Family Management → [your child] → Monthly spending limit
do: Set a monthly limit, or zero.
Remove any saved payment card from the account.

checklist: Child account created and in use
talkAboutIt: Ask who they play with online and whether they’ve met them in person.
Agree a rule about accepting party invites from people they don’t know.
Set the play window together so the console isn’t the one saying no.

xbox.name: Xbox
xbox.blurb: Managed through Microsoft Family Safety, which also covers Windows PCs on the same account.
risks: Voice and text chat with strangers in multiplayer
Cross-network play, which brings in players from other platforms with different rules
Store and in-game spending
beforeYouStart: Your child needs a child Microsoft account inside your family group. An adult account can’t be restricted.
The same settings also cover Minecraft and any Windows PC signed in with that account.

steps.title: Create a child account in your family group
steps.why: The base layer. Without it, none of the controls apply.
steps.path: family.microsoft.com, or the Xbox Family Settings app
do: Sign in at family.microsoft.com with your Microsoft account.
Add your child as a family member with their correct date of birth.
Sign them in on the Xbox with that account.

steps.title: Set access to content by age
steps.why: Blocks games and apps above their rating.
steps.path: family.microsoft.com → [your child] → Content filters → Apps and games
do: Set the age limit for apps and games.
Turn on web filtering if they use the Xbox browser.

steps.title: Set privacy and online safety
steps.why: This is where multiplayer and who can talk to your child is actually decided.
steps.path: account.xbox.com/settings → [your child] → Privacy & online safety → Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, and Windows 10 devices
do: Set 'You can join multiplayer games' according to what you’re comfortable with.
Set 'Others can communicate with voice, text, or invites' to Friends only.
Set 'You can add friends' — block it for younger children so requests come through you.
Decide on cross-network play, which allows players from other platforms.

recommended.0-6: Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block. Cross-network: Block.
recommended.7-11: Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block. Cross-network: Block.
recommended.11-12: Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Block.
recommended.13-15: Communicate: Friends only. Add friends: Allow.

steps.title: Set screen time
steps.why: You can set separate schedules per device, so Xbox and PC don’t share one budget.
do: Set a schedule for the Xbox.
Add multiple time slots in a day if that fits your routine better than one block.

steps.title: Control spending
steps.why: Stops in-game currency purchases turning into a monthly surprise.
do: Turn on 'Needs organizer approval to buy things'.
Turn on purchase notifications.
Consider adding money to their balance rather than leaving a card on the account.

checklist: Child Microsoft account created and in use
App and game age limits set
talkAboutIt: Ask who’s in their party when they play. It’s the fastest way to spot a stranger.
Agree what happens when a friend request comes in from someone they only know in game.
Look at the weekly activity report together rather than alone.

links.label: Xbox — privacy and online safety settings (official)

switch.name: Nintendo Switch
switch.blurb: Controlled through a separate phone app, which is the easiest console setup of the three.
risks: Voice chat in some games happens through a phone app, outside the console’s controls
eShop spending
Sharing screenshots and videos to social media
beforeYouStart: Download the Nintendo Switch Parental Controls app on your phone. It’s separate from the main Nintendo app.
You’ll need the console in front of you once, to link it with a registration code.

steps.title: Link the app to the console
steps.why: Once linked, you manage everything from your phone without touching the console again.
do: Install the Nintendo Switch Parental Controls app and sign in with your Nintendo Account.
The app gives you a registration code.
On the console, go to System Settings, then Parental Controls, and enter the code.
Set a PIN that your child doesn’t know.

steps.title: Set the restriction level
steps.why: The quickest way to match content to their age. You can fine-tune afterwards.
do: Choose the age band that describes your child.
Or choose Custom to set software rating, posting to social media, and communication individually.

steps.title: Restrict communication and social posting
steps.why: Stops screenshots being posted publicly and limits in-game communication with strangers.
do: Turn off Posting to Social Media.
Restrict Communicating with Others.
Note that some games route voice chat through the Nintendo Switch Online phone app, which sits outside these controls, so check that separately.

steps.title: Set a play-time limit and bedtime alarm
steps.why: The console can suspend the game at the limit rather than just showing a message, which removes the argument.
do: Set a daily play-time limit, with different values for weekdays and weekends if you like.
Set a bedtime alarm.
Turn on Suspend Software if you want the limit to be firm rather than advisory.

steps.title: Block eShop spending
steps.why: Set up in a different place from everything else, which is why it gets missed.
do: Sign in at accounts.nintendo.com and open your Family Group.
Select your child and turn on the eShop purchase restriction.
Remove any saved card.

checklist: Parental Controls app linked to the console
Restriction level set for their age
Play-time limit and bedtime alarm set
talkAboutIt: Ask whether any of their games use the phone app for voice chat, since that’s outside these controls.
Agree the play-time limit together so the alarm isn’t a surprise.
Play something together. The Switch is good for that.

links.label: Internet Matters — Nintendo Switch parental controls

firetablet.name: Amazon Fire tablet
firetablet.blurb: Often a child's first tablet. Amazon Kids builds a walled garden with genuinely good controls inside it, and almost none outside it. The lock screen PIN is the whole wall.
risks: Without a lock screen PIN your child simply switches to your profile, where nothing is filtered
Amazon Kids+ is a content subscription, not the safety product. Every control here is free
Filtered browsing filters rather than blocks, and Alexa and pre-installed apps can lead out of the sandbox
beforeYouStart: You'll set this up from your own Amazon account, so have your password to hand.
Decide on a lock screen PIN your child does not know and won't watch you type.

steps.title: Set a lock screen PIN first
steps.why: This is the one that matters. Amazon's own setup guide says it plainly: the PIN is what stops your child getting out of their profile and into yours. Without it everything below is decoration.
steps.path: Settings → Security & Privacy → Lock Screen Passcode
do: Open Settings on the tablet, then Security & Privacy.
Set a lock screen PIN or password.
Use something your child hasn't seen you type, and not a birthday.
steps.result: Switching out of a child profile now needs your PIN.

steps.title: Create a child profile
steps.why: The child profile is the sandbox. Age filters, time limits and the safer browser all live inside it and apply nowhere else.
do: Open the Amazon Kids app, or follow the setup prompts on a new tablet.
Tap Add Child.
Enter their name, date of birth and pick an avatar. You can add up to four children.
steps.note: Amazon Kids is free. Amazon Kids+ is a paid content library on top of it, and buying it adds no extra controls.

steps.title: Set the age filter
steps.why: This is what decides which books, videos and apps your child sees at all.
steps.path: parents.amazon.com → gear icon next to your child → Adjust Age Filter
do: Go to parents.amazon.com or open the Parent Dashboard app.
Click the gear icon next to your child's name.
Choose Adjust Age Filter and set it to their actual age.
steps.note: Setting it above their age to 'give them more choice' is the most common way this gets undone.

steps.title: Decide about the browser
steps.why: The browser reaches everything the app filters don't. For younger children this is the single biggest decision on the tablet.
steps.path: Parent Dashboard → Settings → Fire Tablet Web Browser
do: In the Parent Dashboard, open Settings, then Fire Tablet Web Browser.
Turn the browser off entirely, or pick Hand-Selected Websites & Videos, or Filtered Websites & Videos.
You can add your own allowed or blocked addresses either way.
steps.note: Amazon describes the filtered mode as filtering things like pornography. That is a deliberately narrow claim, so treat it as a filter and not a wall.

steps.title: Set time limits and a bedtime
steps.why: A tablet has no natural stopping point, and a scheduled limit avoids the nightly negotiation.
steps.path: Parent Dashboard → Settings → Daily Screen Time
do: In the Parent Dashboard, open Settings, then Daily Screen Time.
Set a daily limit under Screen time, and a window under Schedule.
If you want reading before games, set goals under Learn First.

recommended.0-6: 45–60 minutes, off an hour before bed
recommended.7-11: 45–60 minutes, off an hour before bed

steps.title: Make app downloads a request
steps.why: Children ask rather than install, and you get a say without having to police it.
do: In the Parent Dashboard, open Content, then Store Access.
Turn on approval for third-party apps and games.
Leave in-app purchases requiring approval, which is the default.
steps.note: You'll get an email or text when they ask, and the app only arrives once you approve.

steps.title: Check what's outside the sandbox
steps.why: Amazon Kids is strong inside the profile and absent outside it. Ten minutes on your own profile is worth more than another setting inside theirs.
do: Open your own adult profile and look at what's installed and signed in.
Remove or sign out of anything you'd rather they didn't find if the PIN ever slips.
Tell your child the PIN exists and why, rather than letting them discover it.

checklist: Lock screen PIN set and known only to you
Child profile created with their real date of birth
talkAboutIt: Show them the Parent Dashboard so it isn't a mystery.
Agree what happens when they want a new app, so it becomes a request rather than a fight.
Ask what they'd do if something on the tablet upset them, and make clear the answer is to tell you.

links.label: Amazon — set up a Fire tablet for kids (official)
Amazon — web browsing controls on Fire Kids tablets (official)

kidsAlt.name: A child profile with Amazon Kids
kidsAlt.what: Amazon Kids is free and gives you the Parent Dashboard: child profiles, age filters, time limits, and adding your own content. Amazon Kids+ is the paid subscription that adds the curated library of books, games and video. Fire Kids tablets come with a subscription in the box.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Amazon lists Kids+ for Canada, Germany, Japan, the UK and the US. Ireland is not on that list, so check before buying a tablet on the strength of it.

whatsapp.name: WhatsApp
whatsapp.blurb: Encrypted messaging, and the app most children move to when they get a phone. For under-13s there is now a parent-managed account with real controls. From 13 there is no supervision at all, and the privacy settings are the whole toolkit.
risks: Anyone with your child's phone number can add them to a group, and the number can never be hidden
Blocking someone does not stop them seeing your child's messages in a group you both share
There is no supervision mode from age 13, so device controls and conversation are the only levers
beforeYouStart: Have your child's phone in your hand for about ten minutes.
If they are under 13, you'll also need your own phone for the parent-managed setup.

steps.title: If they are under 13, use a parent-managed account
steps.why: This is new, and it is the only real supervision WhatsApp offers. Only saved contacts can message them, messages from unknown numbers go to you for approval, and location sharing and disappearing messages are removed entirely.
steps.path: Child's phone: install and register → Parent's phone: scan QR → create parent PIN
do: Install WhatsApp on your child's phone and register their number, entering their real birthday.
On your own phone, scan the QR code shown on theirs.
Create a 6-digit parent PIN. Do not share it with your child.
Enter that PIN on your child's device to finish.
steps.note: Still rolling out by country, so it may not appear yet. It also cannot be applied to an account that already exists, and it switches itself off on their 13th birthday.

steps.title: Check the minimum age, and what most guides get wrong
steps.why: WhatsApp's minimum is 13, including in the EU and UK. It was raised to 16 in Europe in 2018 and has since gone back to 13, so a lot of parenting advice you'll find is out of date.
do: If your child is under 13, the parent-managed account above is the supported route.
If they are 13 or over, there is no supervision available and the steps below are the whole toolkit.
steps.note: From 13 there is no activity reporting, no contact approval and no way for you to see anything. Personal chats are end-to-end encrypted, so WhatsApp cannot read them either.

steps.title: Tighten the four privacy settings
steps.why: The defaults are more open than parents expect. By default anyone can see their profile photo and when they are online, and anyone can add them to a group.
do: Open Settings, then Privacy.
Set Last seen and online, Profile photo, About, and Status one at a time.
Choose My contacts, or My contacts except, rather than Everyone.

recommended.16-17: Agree it together, My contacts is still the sensible floor

steps.title: Restrict who can add them to groups
steps.why: Group invites are the main way strangers reach a child on WhatsApp.
do: Open Settings, then Privacy, then Groups.
Set it to My contacts, or My contacts except.
steps.note: Read this bit carefully. This only stops someone adding them silently. Anyone can still send a group invite link, and your child can join it regardless of this setting. It also does not remove them from groups they are already in.

steps.title: Silence unknown callers
steps.why: Cuts out cold calls from numbers they don't know, which is a common scam and contact route.
steps.path: Settings → Privacy → Calls → Silence unknown callers
do: Open Settings, then Privacy, then Calls.
Turn on Silence unknown callers.

steps.title: Check live location sharing
steps.why: Live location can be shared into a group, which shares it with every member including people your child has never met.
do: Open Settings, then Privacy, then Live location.
If anything is listed, tap Stop sharing.
Agree that live location is for family only.

steps.title: Show them how to block and report
steps.why: The most useful thing on this app is a child who knows what to do without asking first.
do: Open any chat, tap the contact name, and show them Block and Report.
Explain that the person is not told they have been reported.
Agree that anything odd gets screenshotted and shown to you before they block.
steps.note: One real limit worth explaining: blocking someone does not hide their messages inside a group you both belong to, and a group chat cannot be blocked at all.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings only cover this one service. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time, Family Link, Microsoft Family Safety or your console's own controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Under 13: parent-managed account set up with a PIN only you know
Last seen, profile photo, About and Status limited to contacts
They know how to block and report
talkAboutIt: Explain that a group invite link gets past the group setting, so the rule is to ask before joining a group they don't recognise.
Agree what happens if an adult they don't know messages them: screenshot, don't reply, show you.
Point out that their phone number is visible to everyone in any group they join, and it cannot be hidden.

WhatsApp — how to change your privacy settings (official)

kidsAlt.name: A parent-managed account
kidsAlt.what: Announced in March 2026 for under-13s. The account can message and call but not use AI, Channels or Status. You approve who can contact them and which groups they can join, behind a parent PIN. Setting it up means confirming you are an adult with a selfie.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Messages stay end to end encrypted, so you cannot read them. This controls who reaches your child, not what is said. WhatsApp is still rolling it out and has published no country list, so it may not have reached you yet.

twitch.name: Twitch
twitch.blurb: Live streaming with live chat. Twitch added real parental controls in 2026, but the teen has to start the link and can undo it. The setting that matters most is whether your child can go live themselves.
risks: A child streaming themselves is live and unedited to an audience of strangers who can make requests in real time
Controls are opt-in, started by the teen, and the teen can unlink at any time
Anyone can watch Twitch with no account at all, so not making them an account is not a control
beforeYouStart: You need your own Twitch account, separate from your child's.
Your child starts the link from their side, so you'll need them with you.

steps.title: Link your account to theirs in the Family Center
steps.why: Everything else depends on this. Note that your teen starts it, not you, and either of you can unlink later.
steps.path: Teen: Settings → Family Center → sharable link → Parent accepts
do: Ask your child to open Settings, then Family Center, and send you the sharable link.
Open the link on your own Twitch account and accept.
You can link up to ten teen accounts. They can link to only one parent.
steps.note: You'll be emailed if they unlink, but by then the controls are already off. Twitch says these controls are not mandatory for 13 to 17 year olds, so this is a weaker arrangement than Screen Time or Family Link.

steps.title: Stop them going live
steps.why: This is the highest-value control on Twitch. A live feed from a bedroom to strangers, with a chat making requests, is the risk Twitch's own parent guidance circles hardest. It also stops Stories and video uploads.
do: In the Family Center, open Streaming & Video Uploads.
Turn off the ability to go live.

recommended.16-17: Off unless you've talked it through properly

steps.note: Twitch documents viewers daring minors into things on stream, and warns that a full name, school or town said out loud on a live stream cannot be taken back.

steps.title: Turn off direct messages
steps.why: Whispers are Twitch's DMs and are the main private contact route from a stranger.
do: In the Family Center, open Disable DMs and turn whispers off.
On your child's own account, also check Security and Privacy Settings for Block Whispers from Strangers.
steps.note: Twitch's own help pages disagree about whether Block Whispers from Strangers is on by default, so check the toggle rather than assume. Also worth knowing: if your child whispers a stranger, that person can reply for the next 48 hours.

steps.title: Restrict sensitive content from the parent side
steps.why: Under-18 accounts hide some categories by default, but the teen can turn their own protections back off. Setting it from the Family Center is what puts it in your hands instead.
steps.path: Family Center → Protect from Sensitive Content
do: In the Family Center, open Protect from Sensitive Content.
Leave the restrictions on.
steps.note: Be clear with yourself about what this does. Hiding a category removes it from browsing and recommendations. If your child follows a streamer, or goes straight to a channel page, they still see everything.

steps.title: Set a daily time limit
steps.why: Live content has no episode ending. The limit applies across every device they watch on.
do: In the Family Center, open Enact Time Limits.
Set a daily limit.

steps.title: Turn on chat filters on their account
steps.why: These are the most under-used control on Twitch. They follow your child from channel to channel rather than depending on each streamer's moderation.
steps.path: Any channel → Chat settings → Chat Filters
do: On your child's account, open Chat settings on any channel.
Turn on filters for Discrimination, Sexually Explicit Language, Hostility and Profanity.
steps.note: Filters catch categories of language. They do not catch someone being friendly with bad intentions, which is the thing that actually matters.

steps.title: Agree what to report, and read the weekly email
steps.why: You'll get a weekly summary of who they whispered, who they blocked, which channels they watched and what they spent.
do: Read the weekly email when it arrives, and ask about anything you don't recognise.
Agree that any request to do something on camera gets shown to you.
Show them how to report a channel or a user.
steps.note: If an adult makes a sexually suggestive request to your child, report it under Child Endangerment. Twitch escalates those to NCMEC and law enforcement.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings only cover this one service. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time, Family Link, Microsoft Family Safety or your console's own controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Sensitive content restricted from your side
talkAboutIt: Ask which streamers they follow and watch a few minutes with them.
Agree that anything a stream or a chat asks them to do gets shown to you first.
If they want to stream, talk about what is in shot behind them and what their username gives away.
